baer-heitev/1:ב: For benefit. Chayei Adam wrote that in a case of great financial loss or at a time of pressing need, one who is lenient to permit it for benefit and to cast the monetary equivalent of the chametz benefit mixed therein into the Dead Sea has not lost, for he has grounds to rely [see there], and see in Responsa Chacham Tzvi siman 86. And if a prohibition forbidden in any amount became mixed into another cooked dish — which constitutes two minute amounts — Taz in Yoreh De'ah siman 92 infers that if the piece was forbidden in any amount and fell into another pot and they removed it, its discharge does not forbid in any amount, for we do not say two minute amounts; but moist in moist mixed in this manner is forbidden forever in any amount. And see Taz siman 467 note 17. And similarly Shach himself wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 134 note 16, and in Nekudat HaKesef he objected to Taz and labored to reconcile his own words, and Or Zarua ruled to be lenient like Taz — and see Peri To'elet and in Magen Avraham siman 467 note 13 it is explained that their view is the primary halacha like Shach's opinion, and Shach wrote in Nefesh HaChayim that thus spread the ruling among all halachic decisors stringently regarding two minute amounts. And know that moist in moist is forbidden as two minute amounts even according to Taz, as wrote (and in Sefer Or LiYesharim he proved with clear proofs and practical halacha: in a piece forbidden in any amount that fell into another cooked dish — when there is a majority against it, when they identify the piece they remove it; but if they do not identify it, everything is forbidden, and the absorbed quantity in any amount forbids in any amount):
baer-heitev/1:ג: And to sell. See Shach Yoreh De'ah siman 136 that it is forbidden to sell to a gentile except the value of the prohibition therein — whenever the body of the d'oraisa prohibition itself is moist and mixed within it. Chayei Adam [see there]:
baer-heitev/1:ד: That was cooked. Even if a cooked dish that is entirely chametz was cooked in them. And it is permitted l'chatchila to keep them until after Pesach. And if a chametz vessel became mixed, Beit Chadash wrote that it is not nullified, for it is a davar sheyesh lo matirin:
baer-heitev/1:ה: With a peel. It appears rather [one removes] kedei netilah, as explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 105 at the end of siman 461 seif 5:
baer-heitev/2:ב: For detriment. That is, on Erev Pesach, even in less than sixty. Shlah wrote that se'or or chametz cooked with cooked or roasted meat is noten ta'am lifgam and is permitted. See Yoreh De'ah siman 523 — it does not seem so; investigate. Chayei Adam also disagrees in this [see there]:
baer-heitev/3:א: In a chicken. And the same law applies to wheat found on Erev Pesach in baked matzah — it is nullified in sixty even if not removed; but if it cooled before Pesach, it is permitted to eat the matzah and remove the wheat from there even on Pesach. Taz in the name of Beit Chadash:
baer-heitev/3:ב: Reaches yad soledes bo. It implies that in cold one need not forbid; but below siman 467 seif 12 it is explained that even in cold one must forbid. Magen Avraham distinguishes between there and here — and see Chayei Adam. And if [liquid] was poured from kli sheini onto cold, it is permitted if it is not a solid item — see Yoreh De'ah siman 94 seif 7 and siman 467 seif 12:
baer-heitev/4:א: And revives. And it appears [this refers] to the wheat above in seif 3 — that if they heated while the wheat was still inside, for since the substance of the wheat is visible there on Pesach. Peri Chadash wrote: an incident occurred where one loaf of dough was found inside the basket in which they placed matzot as they came out of the oven; they emptied the basket and it was not known which matzah the dough touched — I ruled that one in two nullifies since the mixture was before Pesach, and it is permitted to heat the matzot on Pesach according to all, since there is only flavor; however, all matzot known to have touched the dough require peeling [see there]. And similarly in Sefer Ahavat Chesed siman 99:
baer-heitev/4:ב: Moist in moist. It appears to me that if moist became mixed in moist in less than sixty before Pesach, one may increase upon it a hundredfold until there are sixty so that it will be permitted on Pesach, and this is not [called] nullifying a prohibition l'chatchila — Taz; and see Beit Chadash siman 453 and in Sha'ar HaTziyun there. Flour in flour is called moist in moist, and if nullified a hundredfold it is permitted to bake matzot from it even on Pesach. Terumat HaDeshen, Beit Chadash:
baer-heitev/5:ב: Chametz. It implies that both are required — that it soaked during Pesach and in a chametz vessel — for then we are concerned for discharge of the vessel in cold; which is not so before Pesach, for even in a chametz vessel one need not be stringent, since it is cold and water nullifies the strength of the brine. Or during Pesach in a Yom Tov vessel — plainly permitted, and one need not be concerned for crumbs of chametz in the salt. Later authorities. And if it remained in the vessel twenty-four hours — if it is considered like pickled, see Magen Avraham and Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/5:ד: The meat. That is, dry meat, or even freshly salted meat from salt that was not checked — for their custom is to rinse; and likewise dry fish. But moist salted fish — they did not practice leniency l'chatchila, since they are not customarily rinsed, we are concerned perhaps one will forget and eat without rinsing. Therefore one should not eat pickled lemons on Pesach — Magen Avraham. And Or Zarua wrote that one may be lenient in what they call aksin, for their custom is rinsing; nevertheless they did not practice leniency in any type of salted fish to eat them during Pesach except on the last Yom Tov. B'dieved, or at a time of pressing need, or where Yom Tov joy would be prevented — everything is permitted. Later authorities. And similarly Taz: once there was a shortage of meat and I permitted rinsing fish for Pesach [see there]. And rinsing means soaking somewhat, not merely passing through; and one should soak it in a river or in a Pesach vessel with exchanged water three times, but not in a chametz vessel l'chatchila. Later authorities:
baer-heitev/5:ה: Pesach. But during Pesach one should not soak it; b'dieved one need not be stringent — Maharil wrote that if one did not rinse three times, one may rinse l'chatchila even on Yom Tov, and it is possible even in a chametz vessel if it was not pickled there twenty-four hours — Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/5:ז: One need not be stringent. Meaning: if they already cooked those things, one should not cast them to loss if impossible to keep until after Pesach; and all the more they do not forbid their mixture even in less than sixty, since it is only a rabbinic doubt of a minute amount. And likewise at a time of pressing need or where Yom Tov joy would be prevented — which is like b'dieved. And if there is garlic in butcher goods cut with a chametz knife, Magen Avraham wrote that even b'dieved it is forbidden [see there]:
baer-heitev/5:ט: Beit Yosef. Because of the stringency of chametz we do not say stam vessels are not ben yomo; and even if one says clearly to me that it was not ben yomo, it is forbidden — for a matter not placed upon people is not in their awareness — Bach. It implies that if one cooked it from the outset for Pesach in a vessel that is not ben yomo, it is permitted to eat it on Pesach — Magen Avraham; and it appears to me that one must pour it into a Pesach vessel before Yom Tov:
baer-heitev/5:מ: Two months. And Taz wrote thirty days. Chayei Adam disagrees with him and is stringent like Rama's words:
baer-heitev/7:ב: Clean. It appears to me that this applies to both — that even before Pesach it is forbidden if the vessel was dirty, for even if one would say it is not a davar charif, nevertheless through pressure something enters into it and it is impossible to rinse them — Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/11:ב: On Pesach. Meaning: it became mixed unintentionally on Pesach in sixty and [Pesach] passed; and even if one kept it intentionally, it is permitted, for one did not transgress b'eyna from the Torah in bal yeira'eh, and it is permitted after Pesach even for consumption:
baer-heitev/11:ג: In sixty. This is Tur's view. But all Poskim wrote that we do not require sixty; therefore it appears to me that one who is lenient has not lost even in less than sixty, provided it became mixed in a majority — even for consumption after Pesach — later authorities. And see in Sefer Even HaEzer that he reconciles Tur's view at length in siman 447 Magen Avraham section 4. And if the prohibition is a davar ham'amid, such as beer yeast that passed Pesach and leavened in dough — Or Zarua forbids; R' Meir of Lublin siman 121 (and see Yoreh De'ah siman 123 seif 15 in Shach there). Or Zarua: my ancestor the Gaon ruled regarding butter in which bread or flour soaked and Pesach passed while it remained — one should take the benefit of the bread or flour to the sea or river and sell the butter to a gentile; Chayei Adam in siman 442 wrote that this speaks when water became mixed with the butter, for otherwise it is fruit juice and does not leaven [see there]. And similarly he ruled regarding folded matzah found after Pesach — one casts the fold and also the benefit of the absorbed prohibition for a prutah, and sells the rest to a gentile; but if there were sixty in the matzah against the fold, one casts the fold to the sea and the rest is permitted even for consumption; and the same applies to wheat found in baked matzah; but if puffed, all of it is forbidden forever even for benefit. Chayei Adam in siman 461 is lenient after Pesach [see there]:
baer-heitev/11:ד: The salt. And it is permitted even for consumption if it became mixed after Pesach; which is not so if it became mixed before Pesach in less than sixty — forbidden — Magen Avraham; and see above siman 442 small seif 1:
